en: The Heart Sutra’s underlying meaning is this:
this sutra is fundamentally the wondrous practice cultivated by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the ultimate *nirvāṇa* realized therein.
This wondrous practice consists in practicing profound *prajñā*. This *nirvāṇa* is essentially endowed with the three virtues, namely: the *dharmakāya*, *prajñā*, and [liberation].

Liberation (*vimukti*) is precisely the illumination and vision; the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is precisely the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*); and liberation is precisely the transcendence of suffering. Therefore, it is said:

"Illuminating and seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity. Thus, the Buddha desired that people’s attainment be identical to the attainment of the Bodhisattvas.

Therefore it is said: "Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Yet, fearing that names of "emptiness" and "form" might arise, one may fail to realize that these are identical within their own substance.
Thus it is said: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. Those who wish to attain this simply must, in a single moment, allow no thought to arise.
When the substance is revealed as true permanence, one is immediately named Avalokiteśvara. As for those who are deluded regarding this, their body and mind burn with affliction.
Nevertheless, this constitutes the six realms and four modes of birth.

If you are unable to achieve even a single moment of resonance with this, you should immediately uphold the resolve of a great man (*mahāsattva*), severing the paths of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*). Without falling into speculative views and knowledge, let non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) remain steadfastly before you.
Illuminating this illusory body and mind, they are quiescent in their very place; this is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The solitary manifestation of true emptiness is called the *dharmakāya*. The *dharmakāya* is unattached; this is termed liberation (*vimukti*).

Because the *dharmakāya* is by nature detached from such characteristics as arising, ceasing, and false delusion, it possesses no sense organs, objects, or consciousnesses of the world. Because the *dharmakāya* severs the prior and posterior limits [of time], it possesses no twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time.
Because the *dharmakāya* does not belong to the causes and effects of either the mundane or supramundane realms, it possesses no suffering.
The aggregates, cessation, and the path: the *dharmakāya* is originally and spontaneously perfected. From the outset, it is free from the duality of subject and object in cultivation and realization;
therefore, there is neither wisdom nor attainment. The *dharmakāya* is free from all marks, yet it is not a state of annihilation. Thus, one cultivates through non-cultivation;
this is relying upon the *prajñāpāramitā*. One realizes through non-realization; this is realizing ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Through non-attainment...
It is attained. This attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* enters and exits through the gates of the six sense faculties, pervading the entire Dharma-realm;
it is numinous and unfathomable, and is therefore called the "Great Divine Mantra. Its numinous light shines uniquely, and is therefore called the "Great Illuminating Mantra.
It transcends all numerical measures, and is therefore called the "Unsurpassed Mantra. It cannot be compared to the Three Sages or the Ten Saints, and is therefore called the "Incomparable [Mantra]."
The mantra, etc., transcends names and cuts off meanings; therefore it is said:
*gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
The Concluding Meaning of the Heart Sūtra (End).
Appendix: The Merit of Upholding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Suvīra, saying: "If any bodhisattvas hold in their hands such profound Prajñā..."
The teachings on the pāramitās associated with skillful means:

it should be known that even if such bodhisattvas have not yet received a prophecy from the Buddha in his presence, they have already received a prophecy from the Buddha, or will before long receive a prophecy from the Buddha in his presence.
If such bodhisattvas hold this profound Prajñāpāramitā in their hands, they should...
Knowing that they seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will certainly have no doubt;
they will swiftly sit upon the sublime seat of awakening and quickly attain the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*). As it is further said:

"If a bodhisattva bestows upon sentient beings the teachings of the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), without a mind of stinginess, one should know that before long they shall become a Dharma-teacher."

O King, he has attained mastery over all phenomena. Furthermore, these bodhisattvas who have now attained the perfection of wisdom and are diligently training in it should be known as those who, before long, will be nourished by the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
They are well able to enter into the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and they are constantly able to reveal and manifest that knowledge of all modes.
By means of this, they moisten and satisfy all sentient beings, skillfully analyzing and demonstrating the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma.
O Well-Vigorous One, just as the orb of the sun appears and eclipses all other lights, so too does the *prajñāpāramitā* studied by the Bodhisattva appear in the world. First.
All non-Buddhists are completely eclipsed. When the Prajñāpāramitā practiced by Bodhisattvas appears in the world, it acts as a luminous illumination for sentient beings.

When Bodhisattvas appear in the world, they act as a luminous illumination for the roots of goodness of all sentient beings and serve as a pure field of merit for the multitude of beings. All sentient beings...
It should be venerated; all sentient beings should take refuge in it; all sentient beings should praise it.
If one studies the perfection of wisdom, among all studies it is the most supreme and foremost, the most excellent and subtle.
The unsurpassed is unsurpassed; it is peerless and equal to the unequaled. Furthermore, it enables all who train to reach the ultimate goal and universally to uphold all that is to be learned.
Regarding all training, it can reveal and demonstrate it, subduing all heterodox arguments and false teachings.
If bodhisattvas are able to train in the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will then be able to practice it.
The practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time. Furthermore, the Buddha told Kauśika:

"If sons of good family or daughters of good family, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently cultivate, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, these sons of good family..."
Women and others shall not, in the present life, be harmed by poisons, wounded by weapons, burned by fire, or drowned by water;
they shall not even meet an untimely death from the four hundred and four diseases, except for those karmic results that were already fixed and must be experienced in this very life.
Kausika, if these sons and daughters of good family encounter legal troubles or hostile bandits...
Being oppressed, they should recite and keep this Prajñāpāramitā in mind with a sincere heart.
If [the oppressor] comes to their place, they will ultimately not be punished by him. Why is this?
Kauśika, it is because the majestic power and influence of this Prajñāpāramitā cause such a result. Kauśika, if these sons and daughters of good family should desire...

When one goes to the presence of kings, princes, ministers, and others, and recites this Prajñāpāramitā with a sincere mind, the king and others will surely joyfully inquire after one's welfare, making offerings, showing respect, honoring, and praising them. Why is this?
Kauśika, because these sons and daughters of good family constantly give rise to the minds of loving-kindness,
compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings, Kauśika, these sons and daughters of good family will always achieve such present merits as these.
Kauśika, if these sons and daughters of good family [apply themselves] to this Prajñāpāramitā...

Those sons and daughters of good family who, with a sincere heart, hear, receive and uphold, read and recite, diligently practice and study, contemplate according to the principle, transcribe and explain, and cause these *pāramitās* to be widely disseminated—wherever such persons may be born, they shall [attain... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
They never depart from the ten paths of wholesome action. Whether it be the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments;
the perfection of generosity, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;
or all the gateways of samādhi and dhāraṇī; or omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects—they do not fall away from these.
In the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts— except when intentionally going there to ripen sentient beings—
they are always endowed with all faculties and have no deficiency in their limbs wherever they are born. They never take birth in poverty or low status,
nor among various craftsmen, nor as butchers, fishermen, hunters, thieves, prison guards, or among *pukkasa*s, *caṇḍāla*s, or *śūdra*s engaged in base trades.
In whatever place they are born, they will possess the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary signs, fully adorned and majestic.
All sentient beings who see them will rejoice. They will mostly be reborn in the pure lands of Buddhas, arising by transformation from lotus flowers.
They will not commit any evils and will never be separated from the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva. According to their wishes, they will travel to the realms of all Buddhas.
Kauśika, those sons and daughters of good family shall travel from one buddha-field to another, attending upon and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
they shall bring sentient beings to maturity, purify buddha-fields, hear the true Dharma, and practice according to the teachings, gradually realizing the knowledge of all modes.
Such categories of qualities as these shall be accomplished by them.
...the merit that comes from this. For this reason, Kauśika, if sons of good family or daughters of good family desire to obtain such superior merit in the present and future,
up to and including unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they should never be separated from the mind set on omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), employing the method of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) regarding this Prajñāpāramitā.
They shall wholeheartedly listen to, receive, uphold, read, and recite these profound sūtras of the *Pāramitā*;
they shall diligently practice and study them, contemplate them according to the principle, copy them, explain them, and cause them to be widely disseminated.

Furthermore, with various kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, and canopies, as well as rare and wonderful treasures, music, and lamps, they shall...
As an offering: (The Heavenly Lord’s clan name is Kauśika; his personal name is Śakra Devānām Indra, which translates as "Lord of Gods. He is popularly known as the Jade Emperor).

Furthermore, Kauśika, if good sons and good daughters, with a sincere heart, hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, diligently practice, reflect upon according to the principle, transcribe, explain, and widely disseminate this Prajñāpāramitā, this is—

Whichever lands, countries, or cities these sons and daughters of good family may dwell in, humans and non-humans alike shall not be harmed by any calamities, misfortunes, or epidemics. Why is this, Kauśika?
It is because wherever these sons and daughters of good family reside, they act for the sake of this trichiliocosm and the other ten...
Throughout the boundless worlds, all the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and others, will constantly come to protect, make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise it,
so that no obstacles shall arise for the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, Kauśika, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family...
Women and others, having written down this great king of spells of the Prajñāpāramitā and placed it in a pure location,
shall honor, revere, respect, and praise it; even if they do not hear, receive, uphold, read, or recite it, nor diligently practice and study it,
nor contemplate it according to the truth, nor explain or analyze it for others, nevertheless, the people of that dwelling place, city, district, or royal capital—
They shall not be harmed by non-humans or any other calamities, disasters, or epidemics.

Why is this? Kausika, wherever this great king of mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, resides, it serves as a protection for all the Cāturmahārājika devas of this trichiliocosm, as well as those of all the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions.
Up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, as well as the nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, will constantly come to protect,
make offerings to, revere, honor, and praise them, so that no obstacles may arise for this Great Divine Spell-King,
the Prajñāpāramitā. Kauśika, these sons and daughters of good family who merely write down the Prajñāpāramitā...
If even by merely placing this Great King of Mantras in a pure location, making offerings to it, honoring it, respecting it, and praising it,

one obtains such benefits in the present life, how much more so for those who can hear it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, diligently practice and study it, contemplate it according to the principle,
and extensively explain and analyze it for others? You should know that for such people, merit is boundless and they will swiftly realize Bodhi.
For the benefit and happiness of all. Furthermore, Kauśika, if sons or daughters of good family fear enemies, wild beasts, calamities, or crossroads;

or if they are weary of epidemics, poisons, spells, and the like, they should write down this great king of divine mantras, the Prajñāpāramitā, in portions however large or small, place it within a fragrant pouch, set it inside a precious tube, and carry it with them at all times.
By making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, and praising [this], all matters of fear will naturally be eliminated, for devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts will constantly provide protection.
Kausika, if there are sons or daughters of good family who... [do so].

Furthermore, if any sons of the gods or daughters of the gods hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā* even once, by the power of their roots of goodness, they will certainly and gradually realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is this?

Kauśika, all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as their disciples, have all studied this very Prajñāpāramitā, thereby realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and entering the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder. Why is this?
Kauśika, it is because this Prajñāpāramitā universally encompasses everything.
Because the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), whether they be the dharmas of the Buddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas,
or the dharmas of the śrāvakas, are all subsumed therein— if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should even briefly hear this Prajñāpāramitā,
and having heard it, write it down, read it, recite it, receive and uphold it, contemplate it, and practice it— this son of good family or daughter of good family...
Women and others will swiftly emerge from birth and death and realize *nirvāṇa*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"If a person were to erect stupas made of the seven precious substances for the Buddha, filling a trichiliocosm, each one a yojana in height, and were to offer incense, flowers, necklaces, and music throughout their entire life, the merit obtained would not equal that of a person who copies, receives, and upholds [this sūtra]."
If one reveres, respects, and praises this Prajñā Sūtra, making offerings of flowers, incense, and even music, the merit thereof is exceedingly great.
At that time, the devas and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if there is a person who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and so forth, even correctly recollecting it, we regard such a person as the Buddha himself, or as one next to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is."
It is said: If a person upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and even maintains it through right mindfulness, copies and preserves its scrolls, and honors it with flowers and incense,
this person will be beloved by their parents, cherished by their kinsmen and friends, respected by all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
and esteemed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, as well as by pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and even srotāpannas.
It is revered by all the world— whether devas, māras, brahmās, or asuras—
and even all the devas within the trichiliocosm who have resolved for bodhicitta come to the place where this written scroll of the sutra is kept;
having seen the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, they read, recite, make offerings to it, prostrate, and then depart.

If there is someone who merely copies this sutra scroll and makes offerings to it in their home, yet does not accept it, read it, recite it, explain it, or correctly contemplate it, then neither humans nor non-humans will be able to find an opportunity to harm them in that place.

Furthermore, if one accepts, upholds, and makes offerings to the Prajñā[pāramitā], it is superior to making offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions and their assemblies of disciples. Moreover, if another person writes the Prajñā...
If one gives this sutra scroll to others and causes them to study it, the merit thereof is exceedingly great.

Furthermore, if a person wishes to see the present Buddha’s dharma-body and form-body within the infinite worlds of the ten directions, they should hear, receive, and uphold the *Prajñāpāramitā*, read and recite it, correctly contemplate it, and explain it extensively for others.
This person practicing the *prajñā* should also cultivate the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) in accordance with the Dharma.
...obscure. If one seeks the path of the Buddha, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, or the path of the Śrāvaka, one should in all cases offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one were to transform sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to attain the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), it would not equal the merit of writing down the Prajñā and causing others to read and recite it.
Furthermore, the merit of causing others to read and recite the Prajñā with this [text] does not equal that of right mindfulness (samyaksmṛti).
One should contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, the merit of this correct mindfulness of *prajñā* is not equal to that of explaining it to others so that they may easily understand it.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "Does a bodhisattva practice only the *prajñāpāramitā* and not the other *pāramitās*?
The Buddha said: "A bodhisattva practices all six *pāramitā* dharmas, by way of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)."
Therefore, one practices the perfection of giving, up to and including the practice of the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva does not resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, they will be unable to study the six perfections, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
If one does not study the six *pāramitās*, up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmas*), one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that those regarded as "Buddhas" are those who possess the *dharmatā-kāya*, abide on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and have reached up to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Those regarded as "next to Buddhas" are *māṃsa-kāya* bodhisattvas who are able to expound the *Prajñāpāramitā*. And...
Regarding its correct meaning: A question is asked, "If Prajñā resides within the body of a Buddha, then by making offerings to one Buddha, one makes offerings to Prajñā.

Why, then, is it said that making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions is not as good as making offerings to Prajñā? The answer is: This is because [the former] involves a mind of attachment.
If one makes offerings to a Buddha, one grasps at the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). Yet, a person is ultimately unobtainable. Because one grasps at marks, [the field of merit]—*puṇyakṣetra*.

Although [the former] may be great, its merit is meager. One who makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā does so with a mind that, as taught within the Prajñāpāramitā itself, does not grasp at the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*) nor grasp at the mark of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*); for this reason, their merit is vast.

Furthermore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the teacher of all Buddhas; it is through her that the Buddhas attain the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), as well as immeasurable [qualities].
The light, supernatural powers, and transformations are all due to the power of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For these reasons and conditions, it is superior to making offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is not because one does not revere the Buddhas. Śakra thought to himself:
"If *prajñā* is the ultimate dharma, then one should simply practice *prajñā*; what need is there for other dharmas? The Buddha replied: "A bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās*."
By means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, through the harmony of the dharma of non-apprehension, this is precisely the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one practices only the *prajñā* and does not practice the other five *pāramitās*, then the merit will not be complete;

it will be neither beautiful nor sublime. It is like a foolish person who, not knowing the various ingredients for preparing food and drink, hears that sauce is the master of all flavors, and [thereupon...]
If one drinks only sauce, the flavor is lost and it leads to distress. It is the same for the practitioner:
if they wish to eliminate attachment but practice only Prajñāpāramitā, they will instead fall into wrong views and be unable to advance in wholesome dharmas.
If it is conjoined with the five pāramitās, then its merit is complete and its meaning and flavor are harmonious. Although all practices are combined, Prajñā is the sovereign. If there is giving...
When all phenomena apart from Prajñā are considered, there are various distinctions; yet within the Prajñāpāramitā, they are all of one single mark, without distinction.
Question: To practice the Prajñāpāramitā—whether by receiving, reciting, or even correctly contemplating it—is difficult;
whereas to transcribe the Prajñā sūtra into a volume and give it to others is easy. [The merit of the latter] should not even be compared [to the former].

[The text begins with] "and so forth. Why is it said to be superior? The answer is: although one may recite and study alone with correct mindfulness, because of the presence of a self-centered mind, the merit is small.
One who gives a scripture to another possesses great compassion and creates the causal conditions for the Buddha-way;

because they are free from the notion of "I" and "mine," their merit is great. Furthermore, there is the person who extensively explains its meaning amidst a great assembly; their merit [is likewise great].
It surpasses the former. One should regard such a person as a Buddha, or as one next to a Buddha.
Thus, through various praises of upholding, reciting, and reading the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the merits and roots of goodness obtained in this life and future lives cannot be fully recorded;
they are explained at length in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Formerly, when the Dharma Master Xuanzang traveled to India, he passed through the Moheyan desert on his way. Long...
It was over eight hundred *li* long. In ancient times it was called the Sandy River (*Shāhé*). Above, no birds flew; below, no beasts ran; furthermore, there was neither water nor grass.
At that time, looking at his own reflection, he had but one thought in his mind: he recited only the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.

Previously, while the Dharma Master was in Shu, he saw a sick man whose body was covered in foul-smelling sores and whose clothes were tattered and filthy. Moved by compassion, he took him toward the monastery to provide for him.
He provided the funds for clothing and food. The sick man felt ashamed and presented the *Heart Sūtra* to the Master, entrusting him with it, saying:

"Whenever you encounter difficult circumstances, you should recite this. Because the Master constantly practiced its recitation, when he reached the Shahe (Sandy River) region, he encountered various malevolent spirits and strange, monstrous beings who surrounded people from front and back.
Although he invoked Avalokiteśvara, they could not be entirely dispelled; however, as soon as he recited the *Heart Sūtra*, they fled.
The sounds all dispersed. Having been rescued from peril, I truly relied upon them.
Phonetic Explanation:
*kacaṅgala* (refers to those of low caste who clear away filth and carry corpses); *caṇḍāla* household (a family of executioners); *śūdra* (farmers). Six.
The pāramitās (1. dāna, 2. śīla, 3. kṣānti, 4. vīrya, 5. dhyāna, 6. prajñā).
